newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland schools paid too much in borrowing - paper.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland schools paid too much in borrowing - paper.

text.p: Cleveland school administrators and their financial advisers failed to obtain competitive interest rates in financing computer equipment, borrowing to meet payroll and other deals in the three-year period leading up to the state takeover of the financially strapped district, the Cleveland Plain Dealer reported Tuesday.

Experts retained by the newspaper found that the school system could have cut $1.3 million from its financing costs for computers bought in 1992, the Plain Dealer reported in the last of a three-part series.

J.B. Kurish, executive director of the Municipal Issuer Research and Analysis Center in Chicago, also found that the schools could have saved another $187,000 in a financing to obtian cash in 1992 and as much as $250,000 in last-minute borrowing to meet payroll in December 1994, the Plain Dealer reported.

The district tried, but failed, to obtain credit support for the last-minute borrowing to cover payroll due out in days, the newspaper reported. The borrowing costs reported, including interest rate, sales commission and other expenses exceeded 12 percent, the newspaper reported.
The financing of $75.7 million of bonds in March 1993 has resulted in nearly $700,000 of excessive interest even with bond insurance, the Plain Dealer reported.

McDonald & Company Securities Inc, the district's main underwriter during the period analyzed by the Plain Dealer, has called the school system's borrowing extraordinarily challenging and disputed the findings, the Plain Dealer reported.

While the interest rates and underwriter compensation on deals completed after the state takeover of the system were more favorable to the district than earlier deals, they cannot be compared because each issue is unique and the state takeover changed the whole situation, McDonald's president and chief operating officer told the Plain Dealer.

In a terse statement, McDonald said, "We strongly disagree with the tone and content of The Plain Dealer's articles and are disappointed by the paper's distorted portrayal of our firm's work in public finance."

McDonald's statement continued, "Our disappointment is heightened by the fact that we cooperated extensively with the newspaper in the preparation of its article. We are sorry to learn that our input was given so little weight by The Plain Dealer and that the newspaper opted to abandon any pretense of objectivity in its coverage of this story."

In prior installments of the series, the newspaper also reported that McDonald and Calfee Halter, the district's bond counsel for seven consecutive issues, had contributed about $30,000 to a 1994 district levy referendum.

Employees or political action committees of the two also contributed nearly $37,000 to the "reform" slate of candidates that ran the district during the period and to Mayor Michael White's campaign funds, the Plain Dealer reported.
The newspaper also reported that a firm headed by a financial adviser to the district, Charles E. Brown, had borrowed money from McDonald beginning in April 1993.

Chase Global Securities Inc. served as adviser to securities deals in June 1993 and March 1994 in which McDonald also participated, the Plain Dealer reported. Even after their relationship was disclosed to former school Treasurer William Aldridge later in 1994, he recommended both firms be hired for a December 1994 debt issuance and a 1995 deal never completed because of the state takeover, the newspaper reported.
The relationship between Chase Global and McDonald was not disclosed in the official statement to potential bond buyers, the Plain Dealer reported.
McDonald said its campaign contributions were proper.
